Worst-case Bayes factor: the rival at its most favorable share

Source: R/bf_worst_case.R
bf_worst_case.Rd

A researcher has coded the evidence into two counts: y_W observations support the working theory and y_R support a single rival. One model underlies both Bayes factors in this package. Each observation supports the working theory with probability \(\theta\), the share of the evidence that supports it. The working theory claims \(\theta > 1/2\) and the rival claims \(\theta \le 1/2\).

Usage

bf_worst_case(y_W, y_R, omega = 1, a1 = 1, b1 = 1)

Arguments

y_W

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the working theory.

y_R

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the rival.

omega

Positive number. The bias factor: how many times as likely the search was to find a pro-working-theory observation as a pro-rival one. Default 1, an unbiased search.

a1, b1

Positive numbers. The Beta pair rescaled onto the working theory's shares. Default 1 and 1, uniform weights.

Value

A length-1 numeric: the Bayes factor in favor of the working theory with the rival at its most favorable share.

Details

The numerator is the one bf_uniform_weights() uses: the binomial probability of the counts averaged over the shares above one half. The denominator is the largest probability any weights on the rival's shares can give the counts. When at least as many observations support the working theory as the rival, the probability of the counts rises on the whole of the rival's range, so that largest probability is the one at a share of one half. The value is therefore the smallest Bayes factor a critic can produce by changing only the weights on the rival's shares (supplement, prp-bound). At nine observations for the working theory and three for the rival it is 7814 / 2860 = 2.73.

The paper's rule sets the rival aside, at least provisionally, when the uniform-weights value is 20 or more and this value is above 1. A value above 1 means that no weights on the rival's shares make the counts more probable under the rival than under the working theory.

Closed form

With \(N = y_W + y_R\), uniform weights on the working theory's shares, and no bias, the value is $$\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{y_W} \binom{N+1}{j}}{(N+1)\binom{N}{y_W}}$$ (supplement, thm-closed-form). The paper evaluates the rival at one half at every count, and so does this function when y_W < y_R; at those counts the value is below 1 and the rule keeps the rival whichever share the rival is held at.

Stated weights on the working theory's shares

a1 and b1 replace the uniform weights in the numerator with a Beta\((a_1, b_1)\) distribution rescaled onto the shares above one half: if \(X\) has that distribution, \(\theta = 1/2 + X/2\). Only the working theory's weights enter, because the rival is evaluated at its most favorable share whatever weights its proponent might state. At nine of twelve, Beta(1/2, 1/2) gives 2.07 and Beta(10, 10) gives 4.38. No weights give more than 4.81, the value with all the weight on a share of nine twelfths.

A biased search

A search omega times as likely to find a pro-working-theory observation as a pro-rival one turns a share \(\theta\) of the evidence into a share \(q = \omega\theta / (\omega\theta + 1 - \theta)\) among the observations found. The numerator averages the probability of the counts at \(q\) over the working theory's shares. The rival's shares become shares found of at most \(\omega / (1 + \omega)\), and the counts are most probable at a share found of \(y_W / N\), so the denominator is the probability at whichever of the two is smaller.

Up to \(\omega = y_W / y_R\) that is the probability at a share of one half, which is the value the paper's code computed. Past it the rival's most favorable share is below one half. At nine of twelve and \(\omega = 5\), one half becomes 5/6 found, where nine of twelve has probability 0.197, while a share of 0.375 becomes 0.75 found, where it has probability 0.258; the numerator is 0.0554, so the value is 0.0554 / 0.258 = 0.21 rather than 0.0554 / 0.197 = 0.28. The bias at which the value falls to 1 always comes before \(y_W / y_R\), so sens_bias() gives the same tipping point under either reading.

See also

bf_uniform_weights() for the Bayes factor that averages over the rival's whole range; bf_worst_case_finite() for documents read from an archive of known size; sens_bias() and sens_coding() for the sensitivity analyses.

Examples

# The paper's running example: nine observations support the working
# theory, three support the rival.
bf_worst_case(9, 3)
#> [1] 2.732168

# Seven of twelve falls below one: a rival who may claim an evenly
# split body of evidence is not embarrassed by those counts.
bf_worst_case(7, 5)
#> [1] 0.5644911

# The smoking-gun memo counted as ten observations.
bf_worst_case(18, 3)
#> [1] 143.2847

# Weights on the working theory's shares concentrated near 3/4.
bf_worst_case(9, 3, a1 = 10, b1 = 10)
#> [1] 4.384581

# A search twice as likely to find pro-working-theory evidence.
bf_worst_case(9, 3, omega = 2)
#> [1] 0.6661293
